entries.name: Ex Machina
entries.background: A 2014 film, written and directed by Alex Garland, about a programmer asked to judge whether a humanlike robot called Ava is conscious.

entries.name: Blake Lemoine
entries.background: Google engineer who said in 2022 that the company's chatbot LaMDA was conscious. Google dismissed him for breaching confidentiality.

entries.name: David Chalmers
entries.background: Australian philosopher known for the "hard problem of consciousness", the puzzle of why physical processes give rise to felt experience. He has argued that conscious machines may be possible.

entries.name: Geoffrey Hinton
entries.background: A pioneer of artificial neural networks and Nobel Prize winner who has said AI may already be conscious.

entries.name: Thomas Nagel
entries.background: American philosopher whose 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" defined consciousness as there being something it is like to be a creature.

entries.name: computational functionalism
entries.senseHere: The assumption that running the right kind of information processing, whatever it runs on, is enough to produce consciousness. The author treats it as a hidden assumption behind the idea of conscious AI, and doubts it.
entries.background: In philosophy, functionalism says mental states are defined by what they do, not what they are made of.

entries.name: Turing machine
entries.senseHere: An imaginary device that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape by fixed rules, and so defines what counts as an algorithm. The author calls the world of such step-by-step symbol shuffling "Turing world".

entries.name: substrate independence
entries.senseHere: The idea that a computation does the same thing whatever material runs it. The author prefers "substrate flexible", since not every material, such as cheese, can build a working computer.

entries.name: autopoiesis
entries.senseHere: The way a living cell keeps making and repairing itself, maintaining the conditions for its own continued existence.
entries.background: The word comes from Greek for "self-production" and was coined by Chilean biologists Maturana and Varela.

entries.name: neural replacement thought experiment
entries.senseHere: A thought experiment in which brain parts are swapped one by one for silicon parts that behave identically. It is meant to show consciousness would survive the change.

entries.name: mortal computation
entries.senseHere: Computing whose programs are bound to their particular hardware, so they effectively die when that hardware does. The payoff is saving energy.

entries.name: neuromorphic computation
entries.senseHere: Computing that copies finer details of real neurons, such as the exact timing of their spikes, instead of using simplified artificial neurons.

entries.name: Watt Governor
entries.background: A steam-engine speed regulator: spinning weighted balls swing outward as speed rises and shut a valve. It works by pure mechanics, with no calculation.

entries.name: 4E cognitive science
entries.senseHere: Approaches that see mind as enactive, embodied, embedded and extended, and describe it with continuous changing processes rather than algorithms.

entries.name: biological naturalism
entries.senseHere: The view that being alive is necessary, though perhaps not enough, for consciousness.
entries.background: The name comes from the philosopher John Searle, who held that consciousness is a biological process of the brain, like digestion.

entries.name: predictive processing
entries.senseHere: The theory that the brain constantly guesses the causes of its sensory input and corrects the guesses by the mismatch. The author calls conscious experience a "controlled hallucination", a guess kept in check by incoming signals. Guessing about the body's inner state is called interoceptive inference.

entries.name: simulation is not instantiation
entries.senseHere: A computer simulation of something does not produce the thing itself, unless the thing is itself just computation. A simulated rainstorm gets nothing wet.

entries.name: Nick Bostrom
entries.background: Philosopher who argued we may well be living inside a computer simulation run by advanced descendants.

entries.name: simulation hypothesis
entries.background: The idea that our whole universe may be a computer simulation. Its logic is that simulated worlds could vastly outnumber the original one.

entries.name: Müller-Lyer illusion
entries.background: A classic optical illusion in which two equal lines look unequal because of the arrowheads at their ends. It persists even when you know the truth.

entries.name: Garland test
entries.senseHere: A test, from the film Ex Machina, where you reveal that a being is a machine and see whether a human still feels it is conscious. It measures human persuadability, not machine consciousness.
